sections.heading: Praising you as the Savior who welcomes sinners
sections.text: Lord, you are the Savior of sinners, and I need you. Your name is worthy of honor. Your glory is far above me, yet you come near with compassion that does not run out. You stoop toward people like me with mercy that is gentle and real. Thank you for making yourself known in the gospel—not as a vague hope, but as good news with open arms.
theological_themes: Christ is worthy of praise as the Savior of sinners.
God’s mercy and compassion are not reluctant; he comes near to the undeserving in the gospel.

scripture_references.connection: Paul names the heart of the gospel: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. This grounds the prayer’s direct approach to God as one who saves people who have no claim on him.
God reveals himself as merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and steadfast in love, while still just. That self-revelation supports the prayer’s praise of God’s unfailing compassion and tender mercy.

sections.heading: Thanking you for what the gospel gives
sections.text: Thank you for the discoveries, invitations, and promises you have given in the gospel. In Jesus, rebels are pardoned, captives are set free, the sick are made whole, and the lost are rescued. I come to you through the name of your beloved Son, not trusting my record, my feelings, or my strength, but trusting him.
theological_themes: The gospel offers pardon, freedom, healing, and salvation to those who could not save themselves.
Access to God is through Jesus Christ, not through personal merit.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes his mission in terms of good news, liberty, sight, and release, showing that the gospel addresses the whole misery of sinners before God. This closely fits the prayer’s language of captives, the sick, and the lost receiving salvation.
Paul connects redemption and forgiveness directly to Christ and to the riches of God’s grace. This supports the prayer’s confidence that pardon is found in Jesus rather than earned by the sinner.
Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father. The prayer’s approach to God “through Jesus” rests on Christ’s own teaching about access to God.

sections.heading: Asking to be remade and freed from people-pleasing
sections.text: Please press the likeness of Jesus deeper into my soul again. Lift me above the pull of people’s praise and the sting of their criticism. Teach me to treat human judgment as small compared with your judgment. Let your approval be what I care about most, and let your Word be the rule that guides me when my desires, fears, and the world around me pull in other directions.
theological_themes: Believers are being renewed into the image of Christ.
Faithfulness to God matters more than human approval.
Scripture is the believer’s governing rule for life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that believers are being transformed into the image of the Lord by the Spirit. This grounds the request for Christ’s image to be renewed in the soul.
Paul treats human judgment as limited and looks to the Lord as the final judge who will bring hidden things to light. This supports the prayer’s desire to rise above the smiles and frowns of others.
The psalm presents God’s Word as the light that guides the path of God’s servant. This supports the request that Scripture, rather than moods or social pressure, would govern the believer’s life.

sections.heading: Asking for a life that shows the gospel
sections.text: Make me hate whatever grieves your Holy Spirit. Keep me from mistaking worldly comfort for true comfort from you. Guard me from a careless life. Give me courage to name evil as evil, but keep me humble and gentle when I correct those who oppose the truth. Make me patient with everyone. Do not let me be someone who only says Christian things; make me someone whose life makes the gospel visible—in every relationship, responsibility, season, and circumstance. Let people see in me that your way is good, beautiful, and life-giving.
theological_themes: Holiness includes turning from what grieves the Spirit and refusing a careless life.
Christian correction must be marked by courage, meekness, patience, and love.
The believer’s conduct should commend the gospel, not merely profess it.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit and immediately calls them away from bitterness and toward kindness, forgiveness, and tenderness. This supports the prayer’s desire for holiness that is both morally serious and relationally gentle.
Paul says the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind, patient, and gentle in correction. This directly grounds the prayer’s request to instruct opponents with meekness.
Paul teaches that godly conduct can adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. This supports the prayer’s desire not only to profess the gospel but to display its beauty in ordinary life.

sections.heading: Confessing how far short I have fallen
sections.text: Father, I have not lived up to what I say I believe. I have not made good use of the privileges you have given me. I have served my generation far too little. Too often my words, attitudes, and choices have made my Redeemer look less worthy, not more. Too few people have been helped, strengthened, or blessed through me. In many ways I have sinned, and in everything I fall short of your glory. Please forgive my guilt, because it is great—and because your mercy in Christ is greater still.
theological_themes: Honest confession includes both specific failures and the deeper reality of falling short of God’s glory.
Sin can dishonor Christ before others, while forgiven sinners depend entirely on God’s mercy.
Forgiveness is sought because guilt is real and grace in Christ is sufficient.

scripture_references.connection: James acknowledges that believers stumble in many ways, especially in speech. This supports the prayer’s confession that failure is not theoretical but frequent and concrete.
Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and are justified by grace through Christ’s redemption. This grounds both the confession of falling short and the hope of mercy.
David asks God to pardon his guilt precisely because it is great. This supports the prayer’s unsparing confession without turning away from God’s mercy.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses strong Puritan categories such as rebels, captives, sickness, and lostness to describe the human condition apart from grace. These have been retained in contemporary form rather than softened.

The prayer assumes that a believer’s conduct can either commend or dishonor Christ before others. This is biblically grounded, but it can be pastorally weighty and needed careful wording to avoid implying that Christ’s worth depends on human performance.
significant_interpretive_choices: The opening address, “O Saviour of sinners,” could be read as addressed directly to Christ, while the line about coming in Jesus’ beloved name can sound like prayer to the Father through the Son. The adaptation addresses God personally and explicitly comes through Jesus, preserving the Trinitarian pattern without over-explaining it in the prayer text.

“Re-impress thy image upon my soul” was rendered as asking for the likeness of Jesus to be pressed deeper into the soul, interpreting the image language through the New Testament theme of transformation into Christlikeness.

“Suspect consolations of a worldly nature” was rendered as asking not to mistake worldly comfort for true comfort from God, preserving the original concern about false sources of consolation without suggesting that every earthly comfort is evil.
